extracted.intended_audience: artists, critics, and general readers interested in aesthetics and the evaluation/production of art
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for judging and producing art grounded in Tolstoy's aesthetic theory: what subject-matter, form, and moral aim make a work genuine art rather than a counterfeit. Emphasises infectiousness, universality, simplicity, and alignment with a 'religious perception' of human well-being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art's purpose: uniting men in highest feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: Art unites men. It is desirable that the feelings in which it unites them should be 'the best and highest to which men have risen,' or at least should not run contrary to our perception of what makes for the well-being of ourselves and of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate works by whether they bring people together in morally good feelings (as determined by the prevalent 'religious perception'); example: Dickens' 'Christmas Carol' unites audiences in compassion and love.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable subject-matter: two kinds
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject-matter of what we can esteem as the best art can be of two kinds only: (1) feelings flowing from the highest perception now attainable by man of our right relation to our neighbour and to the Source from which we come; (2) the simple feelings of common life, accessible to everyone—provided that they are such as do not hinder progress towards well-being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Type (1) example: strong religious or ethical feelings; Type (2) includes harmless jokes, folk-stories, nursery rhymes, dolls, etc., so long as the feeling expressed (tenderness, pleasure, humour) 'infects' others and does not obstruct moral progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious perception determines good vs evil in art
rubrics_metrics.description: What are the 'best' feelings? What is good and what is evil? This is decided by 'religious perception.' Some such perception exists in every human being; reason and conscience are always present, active or latent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test subject-matter against contemporary 'religious perception'—i.e., prevailing moral consciousness about human well-being; examples/illustrations include anecdotes (e.g., the cannibal who would not eat his mother) showing an innate moral sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infectiousness: art must transmit feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: The sign of art is infectiousness: art must 'infect' others with the author's feeling — it must transmit a feeling and unite author and audience in that feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A work that does not infect, even if interesting or realistic, is not art. Infection must be actual (felt by audience), not merely admired for craft; examples: the story of Joseph as widely infectious vs. some admired works that only interest or impress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality/Comprehensibility
rubrics_metrics.description: True (universal) art is comprehensible and can infect normal people; works that infect only a small, trained minority are 'exclusive art' and inferior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether a work's feeling reaches beyond an educated elite. Anti-pattern: works that require special training or habituation to be 'infected' (exclusive art, e.g., highly artificial Shakespearean effects as criticised here).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity, compression, and clearness of form
rubrics_metrics.description: Form should possess clearness, simplicity, and compression; the art of the future will be superior in 'clearness, beauty, simplicity, and compression.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate sentence and structural simplicity; long involved sentences and excessive local detail indicate exclusivity. Tolstoy faults even his own 'Resurrection' as lacking sufficient simplicity and compression; simplicity helps achieve universality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty is not a sufficient criterion for art
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty (that which pleases) depends on taste and can furnish no criterion for art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate aesthetic 'beauty' with moral or artistic worth; while beauty naturally accompanies art produced for sincere sharing rather than for hire, it cannot be the definition of art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral/religious aim: art should promote brotherhood and well-being
rubrics_metrics.description: The destiny of art in our time is to transmit from the realm of reason to the realm of feeling the truth that well-being for men consists in being united together, and to set up, in place of the reign of force, the kingdom of love—the highest aim of human life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a work advances the perception that human well-being lies in loving harmony and brotherhood; art that fosters right relations between people is of highest value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progressive nature of art
rubrics_metrics.description: Art is not stationary but progressive: the subject-matter of art improves as humanity's religious perception advances, even if verbal power is not greater than in the past.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider historical development of subject-matter: newer attainments in moral perception can make previous subject-matters obsolete or harmful; art should reflect contemporary moral progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal feeling vs. external moral (art vs. moral science)
rubrics_metrics.description: Art is judged by the feelings it transmits (internal test), not by any moral lesson one may deduce afterwards; pondering consequences belongs to moral science, not to art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not excuse transmissible bad feelings by pointing to an external moral of the story; e.g., Romeo and Juliet may teach a moral about consequences, but the feeling it infects (sensuality) is the artistic subject-matter to be judged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterfeits vs real art — methods (borrowing, imitating, striking, interesting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many works labelled art are counterfeits, produced by borrowing, imitating, striking effects, or merely being interesting, rather than by sincere infectious feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnose counterfeits by identifying reliance on novelty, imitation, 'striking' devices, or mere interest rather than genuine feeling. Causes include professionalism, perverted criticism, and art schools; example discussed: Wagner's 'Nibelung's Ring' seen as a type of counterfeit art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions of infection: individuality, clearness, sincerity
rubrics_metrics.description: For infection to occur, certain conditions are necessary: individuality, clearness, and sincerity (listed as conditions of infection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a work, check for a distinct individual voice (individuality), the clarity with which feeling is expressed, and the author's sincerity; lack of any undermines infectiousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of science and art: art should transmit reason's truths to feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Art's destiny is to transmit from the realm of reason to the realm of feeling the truths about human well-being discovered by science (broadly defined as investigations into results of actions, institutions, and how to live).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether art embodies and communicates reasoned truths about how to live and about moral relations; trivial or purely technical sciences ('pouring liquids,' analysing spectra) are of little use for art unless they address human well-being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility to the masses: art must not be too expensive or unintelligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Real art should be needful for all men; our art is criticized for being too expensive, too unintelligible, and too harmful for the masses—theory of 'the elect' in art is rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a work is practicable and comprehensible for ordinary people, not only for leisured classes; art aimed only at an elite is suspect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of harmful feelings in subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Art of the second acceptable kind must be such as do not hinder progress towards well-being; art that transmits harmful feelings (sensuality, patriotism leading to war, sectarianism, superstition) is bad art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify transmitted feelings that obstruct brotherhood or moral progress (examples: sensual attraction glamorised in Romeo and Juliet; patriotism as preference for one's country leading to murder in war; sectarian Church practices). Such subject-matter lowers artistic worth regardless of craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity/sincerity of the artist
rubrics_metrics.description: Sincerity is essential: works produced for hire, for fame, or from professionalised, specialised habit without sincere desire to share highest feelings tend to be puerile or worthless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor works arising from genuine desire to communicate inner spiritual strength over those produced for payment or prestige; sincerity aids infectiousness and genuine beauty.
